preTestOffScopeDifferences.before: A cutaway reveals the folds of the inner membrane, called cristae. Shape and colors illustrate its structure; this is not a microscopy reconstruction.
preTestOffScopeDifferences.after: A cutaway reveals the two enclosing membranes, the matrix and connected cristae. Shapes, protein sizes and motion are illustrated for exploration; cristae vary between cells.

Cristae are folds of the inner membrane. The rounded pouches remain connected to its boundary through narrow junctions. Their membranes hold much of the machinery for ATP production. Trace the cristae to approach each example fold.
The outer membrane encloses the organelle. A second membrane lies beneath it. Open the cutaway to see the gap between them and the folds extending into the matrix.

A narrow compartment separates the two enclosing membranes. It connects with the spaces inside the cristae. Hydrogen ions pumped across the inner membrane help establish the electrochemical gradient used by ATP synthase.

The matrix occupies the space around the inner membrane folds. It contains enzymes involved in metabolism, mitochondrial ribosomes and DNA packaged with proteins. The small shapes here are illustrative representatives.

The illustrated paired protein heads sit on the matrix side of a curved crista rim. Hydrogen ions passing through the membrane part drive a rotor. That motion supports ATP production in the projecting head. The protein shapes and size are enlarged for inspection.

Compact nucleoids package mitochondrial DNA with proteins in the matrix. The blue bundles mark examples of these DNA–protein structures. Continue inward to explore the double helix in the molecular atlas.

Explore this rounded inner-membrane pouch and the narrow junction joining it to the boundary membrane. Its interior connects to the intermembrane space; the matrix surrounds it. The paired protein shapes illustrate ATP synthase near curved rims. Seven folds form this composed example; crista structure varies between cells.
Move between the enclosing membranes and their folded interior. Follow a crista, inspect the matrix, then trace how a proton gradient helps the molecular machinery produce ATP.

preTestOffScopeDifferences.before: Gold arrow: spring force. Violet arrow: damping force. A dot means zero force.
preTestOffScopeDifferences.after: Gold arrow: spring force. Violet arrow: damping force. A dot marks zero or a force too small to display; read the numbers below.

preTestOffScopeDifferences.before: Right is positive across the deck in this diagram. Forces are for one teaching mode, per unit modal mass.
preTestOffScopeDifferences.after: Right is positive across the deck in this diagram. A dot marks each origin; very short force arrows may be too small to see. Read the numbers for small nonzero forces. Forces are for one teaching mode, per unit modal mass.

preTestOffScopeDifferences.before: 3D arrows show forces on one modal deck mass across the bridge: gold spring, violet damping, white net. A dot marks each origin; arrows disappear at zero force. Arrow length uses its own force scale. The direction stays fixed across the bridge when you turn.
preTestOffScopeDifferences.after: 3D arrows show forces on one modal deck mass across the bridge: gold spring, violet damping, white net. A dot marks each origin; very short arrows may be too small to see. Arrow length uses its own force scale. The direction stays fixed across the bridge when you turn.
Right is positive across the bridge in these rails. Turning the camera does not change this direction.
Circle = ground; diamond = deck. The last rail joins their positions to show the relative gap.
No shaking was applied to this trial. Ground and deck stay at rest throughout the event.
Readings are rounded; the rails use the unrounded positions.
Moving away from zero relative displacement. Spring opposes relative motion: kinetic energy is transferred into elastic energy.
Relative displacement is nearly zero. Spring force is nearly zero, although relative motion can continue.
Damping opposes relative motion and removes mechanical energy.
Damping force and its loss rate are nearly zero.
Direction only; right is positive in this diagram.
The velocity arrow has fixed length. A dot means zero or nearly zero relative velocity; numbers preserve small nonzero readings.
These rates are recomputed from displayed motion. The history interpolates rates recorded at fixed sample times; between samples, its values can differ.
Why can these rates differ from the energy history?
At rest relative to the ground: spring and viscous damping forces are zero.
These are each force’s contributions to relative motion, per kg of modal mass. During shaking, ground input also changes relative kinetic energy.
Relative velocity is nearly zero. A displaced spring can still exert force with almost no energy transfer.
Moving toward zero relative displacement. Spring acts with relative motion: elastic energy is transferred into kinetic energy.
Damping is set to zero, so the damper exerts no force.
Compare visible relief and shadows. Lighting leaves sediment, contacts and clues unchanged.
Speckled tops and lightly textured walls distinguish horizontal and vertical faces.
Surface detail is a visual aid, not evidence of rock type, age or buried finds.
Other rows are hidden for inspection. Displayed side faces are a viewing aid, not newly excavated walls.
Follow one finger from its tip toward the wrist. Use the folds and nails to follow the same hand before and after the turn. Which side faces upward?
The palm side faces upward in both poses. The folds help you follow its surface; the nails mark the back of the hand.
The bar uses all 80 model positions. Resistant share uses living cells only.
